prompt.context: Our client is a large microfinance institution (MFI) in India whose client base — largely rural women earning less than $3 a day — has been growing at over 150% a year. This growth rate is not unusual for private for-profit MFIs in India. However, the rapid growth has started to generate criticism over perceived high interest rates and harsh collection tactics of loan officers. This came to a head when the media and local and state governments began to blame farmer suicides on microfinance-induced over-indebtedness and harsh collection practices.
prompt.question: What should our client do in response to the criticism?

clarifying_info.q: How big is the microfinance market in India?
clarifying_info.a: Microfinance is a huge untapped market. Demand met is $5Bn out of a total $55Bn market.

clarifying_info.q: What is the history of MFIs in India?
clarifying_info.a: MFIs began in the early-to-late 1990s as non-profit NGOs. In the early-to-mid 2000s, many converted to for-profit institutions to access commercial capital and scale.

clarifying_info.q: What interest rates does our client charge?
clarifying_info.a: The average MFI interest rate, including our client's, is between 25-30%.

clarifying_info.q: How many clients does our client serve and where?
clarifying_info.a: At the time of the case, our client provided financial services to around 1 million women clients in 5 states in India.
Loan officers are all from villages themselves and are often incentivized based on number of collections and drop-out rate.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's default rate?

exhibits.title: Math Question — Buffalo ROI
exhibits.shows: A math question asking the candidate to calculate the return on investment for a typical MFI client who buys a buffalo, with supporting numbers provided on request.
exhibits.data: Cost of buffalo: Rs 10,000; Useful life: 1 year (300 days); Maintenance cost: Rs 2/day; Milk yield: 8 litres/day; Market price of milk: Rs 8/litre

exhibits.title: Cost Structure of Client
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart breaking down the cost structure of the client MFI and the resulting cost to borrowers, with labeled cost components and percentage values.
exhibits.data: Personnel Cost: 6.4%; Cost of Funds: 10.7%; Loan Loss Provision: 1.5%; Admin Cost: 3.4%; Profit: 1.6%; Cost to Borrower: 23.6% (equivalent to 12.5% flat rate); note that profit is used for dividends to borrowers and future expansion

exhibits.title: Actual Cost of Borrowing vs. Interest Rates Among Competitors
exhibits.shows: A bar chart comparing the total cost of borrowing (interest rate plus transaction costs and transportation costs) across different providers: government-funded programs (Bank, RRB, Coops, Schemes) and private MFIs (SKS and the client).
exhibits.data: Y-axis: Cost of Borrowing (%) from 0 to 45; competitors shown include Bank, RRB, Coops, Schemes (all government-funded), SKS, and Client; cost components include Interest Rate, Transportation Cost (estimate), and Transaction Costs (bribes, broker fees, etc.)

framework: Market Analysis / Environment: Assess whether this is an industry-wide perception problem; explore government and media motivations (altruistic vs. political); understand competitive landscape (private vs. government MFIs, collection practices, interest rates)
External Response: Launch vigorous PR and marketing campaign emphasizing transparency of rates, comparative cost of borrowing, and client ROI; engage media and press conferences

Internal Response: Implement training programs for loan officers to eliminate harsh collection practices; train area managers on handling press and public criticism; evaluate feasibility of reducing interest rates by analyzing cost structure

questions.prompt: Is the criticism industry-wide or specific to our client? What are the motivations of government critics?
questions.guidance: Strong answer distinguishes between industry-wide reputational risk and client-specific issues. Should note that private MFIs compete with government microfinance programs whose main voter base is rural poor — governments may have political motivations, not purely altruistic ones. Two other private MFIs did engage in harsh collection practices; client has disassociated from them. Other private MFIs are allies in the broader defense of the model.

questions.prompt: Should our client cut interest rates? Walk through the cost structure of the MFI.
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask to see cost structure data. Key insight: admin costs and cost of lending are extremely high; profit margin is less than 2%. This indicates the interest rate is justified by cost structure, not excess profit extraction. Candidate should also examine competitor rates, noting that government programs appear cheaper in headline interest rate but have higher true cost of borrowing when transportation costs and transaction costs (bribes, broker fees) are included. Government programs are also heavily subsidized (World Bank) and have much higher default rates.

math.setup: Read Exhibit 2: Cost to Borrower = 23.6% diminishing (12.5% flat). Breakdown: Cost of Funds 10.7%, Personnel 6.4%, Admin 3.4%, Loan Loss Provision 1.5%, Profit 1.6%.
steps: Profit margin = 1.6 / 23.6 ≈ 6.8% of revenue, but absolute profit is ~1.6% of loan value — very thin
Profit is reinvested: dividends to borrowers and future expansion
math.answer: Interest rate of ~23-25% is almost entirely driven by cost structure; profit is less than 2%, so there is minimal room to cut rates without impacting the organization's ability to scale.

questions.prompt: Calculate the return on investment for a typical MFI client who invests in a buffalo.
questions.guidance: This is the core math question. Candidate should identify ROI formula: (Revenue - Costs - Investment) / Investment. A strong candidate sets up the equation cleanly and arrives at ~86% ROI over one year, which far exceeds the required interest rate of 23-25%, demonstrating clients can comfortably service MFI loans.

math.setup:
ROI = (Revenue - Operating Cost - Investment) / Investment
Revenue = litres/day × days/year × price/litre
Operating Cost = cost/day × days/year
Investment = cost of buffalo
steps: Net return = Rs 19,200 - Rs 600 - Rs 10,000 = Rs 8,600
math.answer: 86% ROI over a 1-year investment period. This is substantially higher than the required interest rate of 23-25%, demonstrating the client can repay loans and still profit significantly.

brainstorming.prompt: Why do you think the ROIs are so high for micro-entrepreneurs?

categories.name: Labor
ideas: Use of family labor that is unpaid and may have no other employment opportunities
No wages paid for household members contributing to the business

categories.name: Infrastructure
ideas: Low infrastructure costs — stores run out of home
Manually operated equipment (e.g., pottery wheels) with minimal capital outlay

categories.name: Tax and Legal
ideas: Operating in the informal economy — taxes and legal costs are not applicable

categories.name: Capital Cost Structure
ideas: Capital costs are a small percentage of total costs
Even at 25-30%, interest on working capital loans represents only 1-4% of income streams and total business costs for poor clients

recommendation: Our client should not reduce interest rates — the 2% profit margin is already thin and is essential to fuel organizational growth and expand access to a larger proportion of rural India's population. Rates are in line with other private MFIs.

Client should launch a vigorous PR and marketing campaign: hold press conferences, engage media interviews, and emphasize transparency of rates, the comparative cost of borrowing vs. competitors (including true cost of government programs), and the high ROI achieved by clients.
Operationally, implement training programs for loan officers to eliminate any harsh collection practices, and train area managers to handle press and public criticism professionally.
risks: If competitor private MFIs drop interest rates, our client may face loss of portfolio and clientele as well as increased criticism from media or government.
Political risk remains elevated given that government programs compete for the same rural voter base.
next_steps: Continue to explore operational innovations to streamline processes and reduce costs, which could eventually allow lower interest rates.
Look into renegotiating cost of lending terms with partner banks (ICICI, HDFC, UTI, SIDBI, and others) to reduce the cost of funds component.
